allCollections.label: Adaptive Learning Systems
allCollections.description: Concepts concerned with systems, models, and design approaches that adjust learning experiences in response to evidence about learners or context.

allCollections.label: Competency and Assessment
allCollections.description: Concepts concerned with defining capability, organizing learning around competency, and collecting evidence of learner knowledge, skill, performance, or outcomes.

allCollections.label: Learning Analytics and Decision Support
allCollections.description: Concepts concerned with analyzing learning data and using evidence, models, interfaces, and analytics to support interpretation and decision making.

entries.definition: A controlled comparison in which two versions of a learning experience, interface, message, or intervention are presented to different groups so their effects can be compared.
entries.why: It gives learning teams a practical way to test design assumptions with evidence instead of relying only on preference or intuition.

entries.definition: The xAPI resource at /about that returns basic information about an LRS, including supported xAPI versions and optional extensions.
entries.why: The About Resource provides a machine-readable way for clients to discover capabilities before exchanging records.

entries.definition: The practice of designing learning technologies, content, and interactions so people with a wide range of abilities can perceive, operate, understand, and use them.
entries.why: Accessibility broadens participation and is part of evaluating whether a learning solution works for the people it is meant to serve.

entries.definition: Testing that checks whether a learning solution can be used by people with different abilities, access needs, contexts, and constraints.
entries.why: It helps teams identify barriers before they become embedded in production systems or learning programs.

entries.definition: An xAPI identity structure that represents an Agent or Group through an account on an existing system using a home page for the account system and a unique account name.
entries.why: Account Objects provide a way to identify Actors when an email address or OpenID is not appropriate, while keeping the identity tied to a known account namespace.

entries.definition: The foundational AI competency level in which teachers develop the essential knowledge, ethical awareness, and practical skills needed to evaluate, select, and use AI tools appropriately.
entries.why: Acquire establishes basic AI literacy and a foundation for more advanced integration of AI into educational practice.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: In xAPI, an Activity is something an Actor interacts with or experiences and that can serve as the object of a tracked Statement. Activities can represent instruction, performance, experiences, resources, events, or even physical or virtual objects.
entries.why: Activities are the primary way xAPI identifies what an experience was about, allowing the same model to describe learning across courses, simulations, work, media, and real-world events.

entries.definition: The optional metadata object within an xAPI Activity that can describe its human-readable name, description, type, more-information location, interaction details, and extensions.
entries.why: Activity Definitions add understandable metadata to stable Activity identifiers without making that metadata the identifier itself.

entries.definition: The xAPI resource at /activities/profile for storing and retrieving generic profile documents associated with an Activity.
entries.why: Activity Profile documents let applications attach durable, application-specific information to an Activity without changing the Activity identifier or Statement model.

entries.definition: The individual or group represented in an xAPI Statement as performing the action described by the Statement.
entries.why: The Actor is the “who” of an xAPI record. Consistent identity modeling is essential for joining learning records across systems and contexts.

entries.definition: A hypermedia system that builds a model of the user and changes the information, links, or presentation shown to that user rather than presenting the same experience to everyone.
entries.why: It represents an early web-based approach to personalization and helped connect intelligent tutoring ideas to online learning.

entries.definition: A learning system that changes content, sequencing, support, feedback, or difficulty in response to evidence about a learner or context.
entries.why: Adaptivity can make instruction more responsive, but it also increases the need for reliable data, transparent rules, and careful evaluation.

entries.definition: Data generated through the routine administration and management of an education system, commonly through education management information systems and related government records.
entries.why: Administrative data is a foundational source for monitoring enrollment, attendance, teachers, infrastructure, progression, and many internationally comparable education indicators.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: A field of computing concerned with recognizing, modeling, or responding to human emotional states and, in some cases, simulating affective behavior in machines.
entries.why: In learning systems, affective signals can inform adaptive responses to states such as boredom, frustration, engagement, or confidence.

entries.definition: The xAPI resource at /agents/profile for storing and retrieving generic profile documents associated with an Agent or Identified Group, independent of a specific Activity or registration.
entries.why: Agent Profile documents can hold information needed by applications without forcing that information into Statements or activity-specific state.

entries.definition: An iterative approach to creating solutions in small increments, learning from feedback, and adapting plans as conditions change.
entries.why: Learning engineering often depends on repeated cycles of creation, implementation, investigation, and refinement rather than one long linear build.

entries.term: AI competency framework for teachers (AI CFT)
entries.definition: A reference framework describing the knowledge, skills, values, and attitudes teachers need to use artificial intelligence safely, effectively, ethically, and in ways that preserve human-centred education.
entries.why: An AI competency framework provides a structured basis for teacher preparation, professional learning, competency assessment, and the development of national or institutional expectations for AI use in education.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: A scaffolded reference pathway for developing AI competency across increasing levels of capability without assuming that development is strictly linear or identical across competency areas.
entries.why: Progression models help organizations plan development and assess growth while recognizing that people can be more advanced in some aspects of AI competency than others.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The extent to which educators can understand and critically examine how an AI system reaches outputs or conclusions sufficiently to assess its use and intervene when necessary.
entries.why: Explainability supports informed human oversight, particularly when AI outputs influence teaching, learning, assessment, or decisions about learners.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The use of AI to support teachers’ lifelong professional learning, collaborative development, reflection, assessment of learning needs, and transformation of professional practice.
entries.why: AI can support professional growth when educators retain control over goals, judgement, collaboration, and the interpretation of recommendations or analytics.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The conceptual knowledge and transferable operational skills needed to understand how AI works and to evaluate, select, use, adapt, or customize AI tools for appropriate purposes.
entries.why: AI competence requires more than operating a tool; it includes understanding technologies well enough to judge their capabilities, limitations, and appropriateness for context.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The foundational set of AI competencies teachers need to understand AI’s human-led nature, recognize benefits and risks, apply core ethical principles, understand basic AI concepts, and use appropriate AI tools in educational practice.
entries.why: Teacher AI literacy provides the baseline needed for safe, ethical, and educationally useful engagement with AI before more advanced integration or creation.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The competencies and practices involved in selecting, validating, and integrating AI with pedagogical methods to support teaching, learning, social interaction, care, and assessment.
entries.why: AI pedagogy focuses attention on when and how AI should support educational practice rather than assuming that the presence of AI creates pedagogical value.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The systematic evaluation of an AI system or tool before educational adoption to determine whether it is sufficiently reliable, trustworthy, safe, ethically compliant, age-appropriate, and pedagogically suitable.
entries.why: Validation creates an institutional checkpoint between the availability of an AI product and its use with learners or educators at scale.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: Teaching in which educators identify and use appropriate AI tools to support activities such as lesson planning, instruction, assessment, and learner support while mitigating associated risks.
entries.why: AI-assisted teaching frames AI as a support to professional practice and requires educators to connect tool use to specific pedagogical needs.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The critical and exploratory use of AI to develop or transform learning scenarios, pedagogical approaches, assessment, and student-centred learning while maintaining human-centred educational principles.
entries.why: At an advanced level, AI can become part of redesigning learning rather than merely automating existing activities, but innovation still requires human judgement and evidence.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The purposeful integration of AI into student-centred learning design and facilitation to support engagement, differentiated learning, teacher–student interaction, critical thinking, and problem-solving.
entries.why: Integration requires aligning AI capabilities with pedagogical principles and learning goals instead of treating AI as an add-on to existing instruction.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: An xAPI Group without its own Inverse Functional Identifier, represented through the Agents listed as its members.
entries.why: Anonymous Groups support recording ad hoc collective activity when there is no durable team identifier available.

entries.definition: A broad class of computational techniques used to perform tasks associated with perception, prediction, classification, generation, decision support, or other forms of intelligent behavior.
entries.why: AI increasingly appears inside learning systems, analytics, content workflows, and adaptive experiences, making governance and evidence especially important.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The collection and interpretation of evidence about knowledge, skill, performance, learner state, or learning outcomes.
entries.why: Assessment data can inform learners, instructors, learning engineers, and systems when it is valid for the decision being made.

entries.definition: An approach that begins with the capabilities and strengths a learner already possesses and focuses on adding new capabilities rather than primarily diagnosing deficits against group averages.
entries.why: An asset model supports individualized growth, lifelong learning, and recognition of strengths that conventional norm-referenced systems may overlook.

entries.definition: Learning activity that can occur at different times, allowing learners to engage with materials or tasks without everyone participating simultaneously.
entries.why: Asynchronous formats provide flexibility and independent pacing, but they require careful design for guidance, interaction, and learner self-management.

entries.definition: A file or other binary resource logically associated with an xAPI Statement, described by metadata including usage type, display name, content type, length, SHA-2 hash, and optionally a file URL.
entries.why: Attachments allow evidence such as certificates, essays, images, or other artifacts to travel with or be referenced from a Learning Record while preserving integrity checks.

entries.definition: The selective allocation of cognitive resources to information, tasks, or stimuli.
entries.why: Learning design competes for limited attention, so interfaces and experiences should reduce unnecessary distraction and focus effort on the learning task.

entries.definition: Foundational and broad fields of study intended to develop general knowledge, literacies, cultural understanding, and core academic capabilities across areas such as language, mathematics, science, humanities, arts, health, and civic learning.
entries.why: These subjects provide much of the common academic and cultural foundation upon which more specialized learning is built.

entries.definition: A field that studies systematic biases, heuristics, and decision patterns that cause people to make choices that depart from purely rational models.
entries.why: Learning designers can use behavioral economics to account for real-world decision behavior instead of assuming learners will always act rationally on information.

entries.definition: A systematic distortion in data, measurement, analysis, models, processes, or decisions that can produce unfair or misleading results.
entries.why: Bias can enter learning systems through data collection, model design, assessment, interfaces, or operational decisions.

entries.definition: The development of increasingly organized, retrievable, and usable knowledge and skill within a domain through experience and practice.
entries.why: Expertise changes how learners perceive problems, use prior knowledge, and allocate attention, which affects how instruction should be designed.

entries.definition: The stage of learning engineering in which a team frames the problem, context, stakeholders, constraints, and evidence before designing a solution.
entries.why: Clear problem framing prevents teams from optimizing the wrong thing or treating a symptom as the underlying learning challenge.

entries.definition: The degree to which a learner actively thinks about, applies, analyzes, and connects knowledge rather than only receiving or memorizing information.
entries.why: Deeper cognitive engagement supports stronger understanding and more flexible application of knowledge and skills.

entries.definition: The mental effort required to process information in working memory during a task.
entries.why: Learning experiences can fail when unnecessary complexity consumes limited cognitive capacity that should be available for learning.

entries.definition: A family of methods for identifying the knowledge, decisions, cues, strategies, and mental processes involved in performing complex tasks.
entries.why: It helps learning teams make expert thinking visible so training can address more than observable steps.

entries.definition: A usability inspection method in which evaluators step through a task from the perspective of a user and ask whether each action is understandable and discoverable.
entries.why: It is useful for finding interaction barriers before or alongside direct user testing.

entries.definition: A community in which people learn through social participation in a shared practice, developing knowledge through interaction with others engaged in related work or activity.
entries.why: Communities of practice situate learning in participation, relationships, and authentic practice rather than treating knowledge as isolated information.

entries.definition: A defined capability, skill, knowledge area, or observable performance that can be described, assessed, developed, or referenced across systems.
entries.why: Shared competency definitions help connect learning resources, evidence, credentials, and workforce requirements.

entries.definition: An approach in which progress is organized around demonstrated mastery of defined competencies rather than primarily around time spent in a course or program.
entries.why: Competency-based learning can connect assessment, personalization, credentials, and talent systems around evidence of what a learner can actually do.

entries.definition: The use of computers to access training or education through synchronous or asynchronous activities delivered on networked or standalone systems.
entries.why: It is a foundational category in the evolution from early computer-assisted instruction to networked and adaptive learning systems.

entries.definition: A representation that shows how concepts or abstract ideas are connected to one another.
entries.why: Concept maps can make relationships among ideas visible and help learners organize knowledge into a more coherent structure.

entries.definition: Knowledge of the ideas, relationships, and underlying reasons that explain why a procedure, principle, or solution works.
entries.why: Conceptual knowledge helps learners move beyond memorized procedures and apply what they know in new or authentic contexts.

entries.definition: A learning theory that treats knowledge as distributed across networks of connections and emphasizes continual learning, current information, and the ability to recognize connections among sources and fields.
entries.why: Connectivism provides a conceptual basis for networked learning environments where knowledge is not confined to one instructor, course, or institution.

entries.definition: A massive open online course organized around connectivist principles, emphasizing networks, social learning, cooperation, and collaborative knowledge construction.
entries.why: cMOOCs highlight a networked model in which learning emerges through connections among people, information, and communities.

entries.definition: Activity references included in an xAPI Statement Context to express how the recorded experience relates to broader or associated Activities.
entries.why: Context Activities make it possible to connect a fine-grained event to a course, program, grouping, category, or other surrounding experience without changing the Statement Object.

entries.definition: An xAPI context structure that represents a Statement-specific relationship between the Statement and a relevant Agent, optionally characterized by one or more relationship-type IRIs.
entries.why: Context Agents allow people who influenced or participated in an experience to be represented without incorrectly making them the primary Actor.

entries.definition: An xAPI context structure that represents a Statement-specific relationship between the Statement and a relevant Group, optionally characterized by one or more relationship-type IRIs.
entries.why: Context Groups make team, cohort, organization, or other group relationships explicit in a structured way within a Statement.

entries.definition: The optional xAPI Statement component used to add surrounding information about an experience, such as registration, related activities, relevant Agents or Groups, language, platform, another Statement, or extensions.
entries.why: Context lets the same core Actor-Verb-Object event be interpreted within a broader learning, organizational, technical, or situational setting.

entries.definition: A condition surrounding a design, such as learner needs, curriculum structure, timeline, resources, or technology, that can influence what is feasible or appropriate.
entries.why: Learning design is situated. Contextual factors can change over time and may cause teams to revisit decisions that were reasonable under earlier conditions.

entries.definition: An ongoing practice of using evidence and feedback to refine learning experiences, systems, processes, and operations over time.
entries.why: Learning conditions change, so effective systems need mechanisms for learning from use rather than assuming the first release is final.

entries.definition: A software development practice in which changes are integrated and tested frequently rather than accumulated into large, infrequent releases.
entries.why: For learning technology teams, continuous integration can make iterative development safer and shorten the feedback loop between change and validation.

entries.definition: An engineering field concerned with how systems use feedback to regulate behavior and move toward desired states.
entries.why: Feedback mechanisms are central to adaptive learning, monitoring, and iterative improvement in complex learning systems.

entries.definition: A managed set of defined terms and identifiers used consistently within a domain so that people and machines can refer to the same concepts in the same way.
entries.why: One of the explicit goals of xAPI Profiles is to provide a common way to express controlled vocabularies for reusable xAPI concepts.

entries.definition: The advanced AI competency level in which teachers critically and creatively configure, adapt, or co-create AI-enabled approaches, tools, policies, and pedagogical practices for educational transformation.
entries.why: Create emphasizes expert judgement, innovation, ethical co-creation, and adaptation to local educational needs rather than simple tool proficiency.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The part of the learning engineering process in which a team creates a response to a learning challenge by designing the solution, planning and instrumenting the needed data, and iterating the design with learners and stakeholders.
entries.why: Treating instrumentation and iteration as part of creation helps ensure that a solution is designed to generate useful evidence from the start.

entries.definition: Collaboration among people from different professional disciplines who contribute distinct expertise to a learning engineering challenge.
entries.why: Learning engineering is multidisciplinary; shared language and clear interfaces between disciplines reduce coordination failures.

entries.definition: A regional or international learning assessment that uses a common agreed framework and similar procedures across participating systems to produce comparable learning-outcome data.
entries.why: Cross-national assessments support comparison across education systems and can provide contextual information about students, teachers, schools, and equity.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: The deliberate effort to shift shared assumptions, behaviors, norms, incentives, and ways of working so an organization can adopt and sustain a new model of learning.
entries.why: Technology and policy changes can fail when organizational culture continues to reward old behaviors or resists experimentation and new forms of collaboration.

entries.definition: The planned subjects and learning content of an educational program, including how instructional time is allocated and how learning is sequenced.
entries.why: Curriculum translates educational goals into an organized program of content, experiences, and progression for learners.
entries.aka: Course content; programme of study; syllabus

entries.definition: The interpretation of data to derive insights, identify trends, evaluate outcomes, diagnose drivers, and assess policy effects.
entries.why: Analysis turns collected education data into information that can reveal achievements, problems, disparities, and possible causes.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: The use of methods and tools to examine data in order to describe patterns, test hypotheses, identify relationships, or support decisions.
entries.why: Analytics turns instrumented learning activity into evidence that can inform design, operations, and evaluation.

entries.definition: The condition in which data exists and can be accessed or retrieved, regardless of whether it has been officially reported or whether its quality is sufficient for a particular use.
entries.why: Separating availability from reporting helps diagnose whether a data problem is caused by missing collection, limited access, weak quality, or failure to publish and share existing data.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: An organizational and institutional environment in which transparency, collaboration, participation, openness, shared definitions, and the regular use of evidence support decision-making.
entries.why: A data culture affects whether investments in data systems translate into routine use, shared understanding, accountability, and policy action.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: The deliberate design and implementation of mechanisms that capture events, states, context, and other data needed to understand a learning system.
entries.why: If the right evidence is not instrumented at the source, later analytics cannot reconstruct it reliably.

entries.definition: The use of computational methods to discover patterns, structures, associations, or predictive relationships in large datasets.
entries.why: In learning analytics, data mining can surface patterns that merit investigation, while interpretation still requires domain and measurement knowledge.

entries.definition: The rights, responsibilities, and governance questions associated with control over data generated or used within education systems.
entries.why: As education systems collect more digital data, decisions about who controls that data and how it may be used become central governance questions.

entries.definition: A sequence of processes that moves, validates, transforms, enriches, stores, or routes data from source systems to destinations.
entries.why: Learning data often crosses many systems, so pipeline design affects quality, latency, traceability, and interoperability.

entries.definition: The principles and practices that govern how information about people is collected, used, shared, retained, protected, and deleted.
entries.why: Learning systems can capture detailed behavioral data, so privacy must be designed into instrumentation and analytics from the start.

entries.definition: The degree to which data is accurate, complete, consistent, timely, valid, and fit for its intended use.
entries.why: Poor-quality learning data can produce misleading analytics, weak automation, and bad decisions even when the underlying technology works correctly.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: The official sharing of available data with the public, international organizations, or other stakeholders.
entries.why: Data may exist without being reported, so reporting capacity is a distinct part of whether education information can support transparency, comparison, and coordinated action.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: The practices and controls used to protect learning data, systems, interfaces, storage, and communications from unauthorized access, manipulation, loss, or disruption.
entries.why: Connected learning ecosystems increase the amount and mobility of learner data, making security a system-wide design and governance requirement.

entries.definition: An isolated store of data that does not readily exchange information with other applications, systems, or organizational data sources.
entries.why: Data silos make it harder to combine information across an education ecosystem and limit the value of data for coordinated decisions and services.

entries.definition: The organizational responsibility for governing how data is held, protected, accessed, shared, maintained, and used across its lifecycle.
entries.why: Learning ecosystems cross organizational boundaries, so responsible data use depends on clear stewardship roles as well as technical interoperability.

entries.definition: The application of data and analytical findings to policy and programme development, resource allocation, planning, implementation, and other decisions intended to improve education.
entries.why: Data systems create public value when their outputs are understandable and actionable enough to influence decisions and practice.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: A decision process that uses relevant data as evidence while also considering context, expertise, goals, and constraints.
entries.why: Data can improve decisions without pretending that metrics alone contain the full meaning of a learning situation.

entries.definition: The use of data, analytics, models, or software to help people make informed decisions without necessarily automating the decision itself.
entries.why: In learning engineering, decision support can help instructors, designers, administrators, and learners interpret evidence and choose actions.

entries.definition: The practice of recording design decisions, their justifications, sources of influence, and revisions across the life of a design project.
entries.why: A persistent record lets teams communicate why a design looks the way it does, revisit alternatives, and connect later changes to earlier reasoning.

entries.definition: The intermediate AI competency level in which teachers integrate AI into educational practice with greater attention to human accountability, safe and responsible use, ethical evaluation, and pedagogical design.
entries.why: Deepen moves beyond basic literacy toward sustained, context-aware use of AI in teaching, learning, and professional practice.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: A choice about what to include in a learning design and how that choice will be enacted, made in response to goals, evidence, experience, constraints, and context.
entries.why: Learning designs are built through many such choices. Making the choices visible helps teams explain, revisit, and improve the work over time.

entries.definition: The process of forming, enacting, communicating, revisiting, and sometimes revising choices about a learning design while accounting for learners, stakeholders, evidence, technology, and context.
entries.why: Tracking decision-making makes design reasoning more transparent and supports iteration across people, project phases, and learning engineering cycles.

entries.definition: The reasoning used to determine why a design choice is appropriate in a particular situation, drawing on knowledge, experience, theory, and contextual factors.
entries.why: Design work rarely reduces to a fixed procedure. Judgment connects professional knowledge with the realities and constraints of a specific learning context.

entries.definition: The recorded reason, evidence, or source of influence that explains why a design decision was made or revised.
entries.why: A decision without its reasoning is difficult for another person to interpret later. Capturing justification supports communication, continuity, and future iteration.

entries.definition: A reusable description of a recurring design problem and a proven or commonly useful way of addressing it.
entries.why: Patterns help teams share solutions and reasoning across projects without requiring every design decision to be rediscovered from scratch.

entries.definition: A change to something previously decided or to an existing element of a learning design.
entries.why: Revisions make iteration visible. Tracking them connects changes to the evidence, experience, requirements, technology, or context that prompted reconsideration.

entries.definition: An iterative cycle in which a learning solution is designed, built, tried with learners or stakeholders, examined through evidence, and revised rather than treated as complete after a single design pass.
entries.why: Repeated design-build cycles make learner and stakeholder feedback part of development and support faster correction of weak assumptions.

entries.definition: A digitally represented claim about achievement, qualification, skill, identity, participation, or authorization that can be issued and verified electronically.
entries.why: Credentials become more useful when their claims can connect to shared competency definitions and interoperable learner records.

entries.definition: Inequality in access to technology infrastructure and in the skills needed to benefit from digital technologies.
entries.why: The source distinguishes an access divide from a skills divide, making digital inclusion a question of both connectivity and the capacity to use technology effectively.

entries.definition: The application of digital engineering methods, models, interfaces, and lifecycle thinking to the design and operation of learning systems.
entries.why: It helps connect learning design to technical architecture, data, testing, deployment, and sustainment.

entries.definition: Data produced through the use of technology in teaching and learning that can be collected, analyzed, and shared.
entries.why: Digital learning activity generates data that can inform decisions, but the same data creates obligations around privacy, ownership, and security.

entries.definition: Reusable digital resources intended for broad public benefit, including research, digital resources and applications, databases, repositories, standards, algorithms, and platforms that can be adapted across contexts.
entries.why: Digital global public goods can reduce duplicated effort and give education systems a shared base that can be adapted to local needs.

entries.definition: Digital content and resources used to support teaching and learning, including digital textbooks, simulations, games, user-created content, and open educational resources.
entries.why: Digital learning materials expand the forms in which instructional content can be accessed, created, shared, and adapted.

entries.definition: The capabilities needed to benefit from digital technologies and to use them effectively in learning and teaching, including the use of digital pedagogies rather than technology use alone.
entries.why: The source frames digital literacy as a second dimension of the digital divide: participation depends on capabilities as well as access.

entries.definition: The protection of digital systems and education data from risks that can undermine confidentiality, integrity, availability, or safe use.
entries.why: The expansion of data-intensive EdTech introduces security risks that education policy and governance must address alongside privacy and ownership.

entries.definition: Skills for using digital technologies, ranging from basic technology competencies to higher-order capabilities such as coding, computational thinking, and ethics.
entries.why: Access alone does not produce effective participation in digital learning. Learners and educators also need skills that let them use technology productively and responsibly.

entries.definition: Learning delivered beyond a single physical classroom through distributed technologies and environments, including distance education, online learning, simulations, mobile learning, and other network-enabled experiences.
entries.why: The term connects the history of distance education with today's broader ecosystem of digital, mobile, simulated, and networked learning.

entries.definition: Simulation conducted across networked systems so multiple participants or simulated entities can interact within a shared scenario or synthetic environment.
entries.why: Distributed simulation supports collective and team-based training and helped drive interoperability standards such as DIS and HLA.

entries.definition: An xAPI construct for storing document-style information about an Agent or Activity in name-and-document pairs meaningful to an instructional system component. It is distinct from an xAPI Profile.
entries.why: The distinction prevents confusion between profile documents used as storage and xAPI Profiles used to constrain vocabularies, templates, and patterns.

entries.definition: The network of public, private, academic, civil-society, donor, school, family, and learner stakeholders involved in developing, providing, governing, and using education technology.
entries.why: EdTech implementation depends on relationships among many actors, which makes ecosystem coordination a core systems and governance concern.

entries.definition: The process through which people develop abilities, attitudes, knowledge, and forms of behavior that are valued within the society in which they live.
entries.why: Education provides the broad frame for how people develop knowledge, skills, capabilities, values, and behaviors across formal, nonformal, and informal settings.

entries.definition: A recurring sequence in which education data is produced and made available, reported and shared, analyzed, and then used to inform decisions and further data needs.
entries.why: The cycle emphasizes that collecting data is only one stage of an effective data system; value emerges when data moves through reporting, analysis, and use.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: The interconnected set of data sources, production and reporting processes, analytical practices, institutions, and uses that together support evidence-based decision-making in an education system.
entries.why: Viewing education data as an ecosystem shifts attention from isolated datasets to the relationships among production, sharing, analysis, governance, and policy use.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: The combination and linkage of data from different education and related sources to create a more coherent view, fill information gaps, and support analysis that a single source cannot provide.
entries.why: Integrated data can connect administrative records, assessments, surveys, finance, and other sources to answer policy questions that span institutional and data boundaries.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: Financial data describing income and spending related to education from public, private, household, and other sources, including spending on infrastructure, personnel, and other education costs.
entries.why: Expenditure data connects resource allocation with education provision and outcomes and is necessary for monitoring the financial dimension of education systems.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: An information system used by education authorities to collect, process, analyze, monitor, and disseminate administrative data for education management and planning.
entries.why: An EMIS is a core infrastructure component for national education data, supporting routine administration, indicator production, planning, and integration with other data sources.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: The capability of an education system to produce, report, assess, and use education data of sufficient coverage and quality to generate indicators and support policy and governance.
entries.why: Statistical capacity determines whether an education system can reliably monitor itself, meet national information needs, and contribute comparable data for international monitoring.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment
UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: The use of hardware, software, digital content, data, and information systems in education to support teaching, learning, education management, and delivery.
entries.why: EdTech is a broad systems concept that includes far more than devices. It connects instructional practice, content, data, infrastructure, and education management.

entries.definition: The organization and administration of part or all of an education system, including the structures and processes used to coordinate, regulate, supervise, and support educational activity.
entries.why: Administration turns educational policy and institutional responsibilities into coordinated structures, processes, and services.

entries.definition: The systematic assessment of educational performance or quality, including evaluation of learners, teachers, curricula, prior learning, institutions, and educational outcomes.
entries.why: Educational evaluation provides evidence for judging learning, instructional quality, program effectiveness, and institutional performance.

entries.definition: The physical and material resources that support education, including buildings, equipment, learning resources, playgrounds, and other academic or school facilities.
entries.why: Facilities shape access, safety, usability, participation, and the conditions under which teaching and learning take place.

entries.definition: Organizations and establishments that provide education, including schools, higher education institutions, training centers, adult education institutions, and other settings in which organized learning takes place.
entries.why: Educational institutions are the organizational settings through which much formal and nonformal education is designed, delivered, supported, and recognized.

entries.definition: The management of educational establishments, including the academic, operational, staffing, resource, attendance, financial, and organizational activities needed to run them.
entries.why: Educational management concerns the day-to-day and strategic operation of institutions that deliver education.

entries.definition: The systematic process of analyzing educational needs, setting goals and priorities, anticipating future requirements, and organizing resources and actions to improve an education system.
entries.why: Planning connects educational goals to the people, resources, timelines, data, and institutional changes needed to achieve them.

entries.definition: The goals, principles, and official directions that guide an education system and shape decisions about access, rights, priorities, standards, resources, and reform.
entries.why: Educational policy establishes the public goals and rules within which education systems, institutions, and programs operate.

entries.definition: The people who participate in and support education systems, including learners, teachers, administrators, advisers, planners, support staff, and other educational personnel.
entries.why: Education systems depend on multiple populations whose roles, needs, relationships, and participation shape how learning is delivered and experienced.

entries.definition: The interdisciplinary study of education and the environments in which teaching and learning occur, including pedagogical, psychological, social, historical, philosophical, cultural, and contextual influences.
entries.why: It connects the study of learning and education with the human and environmental conditions that shape educational practice and outcomes.

entries.definition: The organized structures through which formal and nonformal education is provided, including the institutions, programs, pathways, and successive stages or levels that make up an education system.
entries.why: This concept provides a way to describe how education is organized across institutions and across stages such as early childhood, primary, secondary, and higher education.

entries.definition: The effort to understand users’ needs, experiences, constraints, motivations, and contexts from their point of view.
entries.why: Human-centered learning design begins with evidence about the people and environments a solution is intended to support.

entries.definition: A structured technique for organizing observations about what users say, do, think, feel, need, or experience.
entries.why: It helps teams turn qualitative research into a shared picture that can inform design priorities and hypotheses.

entries.definition: An entry point used for communication with a service. In xAPI, resource locations are exposed through IRIs or URLs rooted at an LRS endpoint.
entries.why: Endpoints define where interoperable systems send and retrieve records and related resources, separating the communication contract from a specific product implementation.

entries.definition: A problem-solving process that develops and evaluates solutions against requirements, evidence, constraints, interfaces, and tradeoffs.
entries.why: Learning engineering uses engineering methods to make learning solutions testable, improvable, and sustainable at system scale.

entries.definition: An organizational record that integrates learner-related data across experiences, systems, programs, or time.
entries.why: Enterprise records can support continuity and analytics across a learning ecosystem when the data model and governance allow systems to interoperate.

entries.definition: The consideration of whether learning opportunities, technologies, processes, and outcomes fairly account for different needs and conditions.
entries.why: A system can be technically functional while still distributing access, burden, or benefit unevenly across learners.

entries.definition: An approach in which ethical requirements are intentionally built into the design and validation of AI systems rather than addressed only after deployment.
entries.why: Embedding ethical requirements before adoption can reduce risks to human rights, safety, privacy, inclusion, and accountability in educational settings.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The body of ethical values, principles, regulations, institutional rules, and practical guidance used to evaluate and govern the design and use of artificial intelligence.
entries.why: For educators, AI ethics connects abstract principles to decisions about tools, data, human rights, inclusion, safety, and responsible educational practice.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The use of data and evidence to inform decisions about teaching, learning, programs, policy, and the management of education systems.
entries.why: Evidence-based decision making connects data collection to iterative improvement rather than treating data as an end in itself.

entries.definition: The use of credible research and empirical evidence to inform the design, implementation, and refinement of learning experiences and systems.
entries.why: It connects learning engineering decisions to established knowledge while still allowing local testing and iteration.

entries.definition: A learning technology specification standardized in the IEEE 9274 family for representing and exchanging records of learning and performance experiences.
entries.why: xAPI allows learning activity data to move across platforms and contexts using a shared statement model.

entries.definition: A design practice focused on shaping the sensory, emotional, cognitive, behavioral, and social qualities of an experience so it becomes more meaningful and memorable.
entries.why: Learning experience design can borrow experience-design methods to account for motivation, emotion, context, identity, and social connection in addition to cognition.

entries.definition: Learning in which knowledge is created through experience and reflection, often described as a recursive process of experiencing, reflecting, thinking, and acting.
entries.why: It provides a foundation for designing practice-rich learning that connects action to interpretation and transfer.

entries.definition: A large-scale open online course model that retains open access and scale while generally using more traditional instructivist course structures.
entries.why: The distinction between xMOOCs and cMOOCs shows how similar delivery platforms can embody very different instructional philosophies.

entries.definition: A concrete artifact, such as a sketch, model, concept map, or prototype, that makes design thinking visible so it can support reflection, communication, collaboration, and iteration.
entries.why: External representations move design knowledge out of an individual designer's head and give a team something persistent to examine, discuss, and revise.

entries.definition: Mental effort caused by features of a task or presentation that do not directly support the learning goal.
entries.why: Reducing unnecessary complexity can preserve cognitive resources for understanding, practice, and problem solving.

entries.definition: The evaluation of whether data, models, assessments, processes, or decisions treat people and groups appropriately under relevant criteria.
entries.why: Learning analytics and AI can amplify inequities when fairness is not examined as part of design and evaluation.

entries.definition: A cycle in which information about outcomes or system behavior is returned to learners, instructors, designers, or systems and used to influence subsequent action.
entries.why: Learning engineering depends on feedback loops for adaptation, monitoring, and continuous improvement.

entries.definition: An instructional approach that moves direct content delivery outside class time and uses shared face-to-face time for more interactive learning activities.
entries.why: The flipped classroom shows how digital delivery can change the purpose of classroom time rather than simply digitizing traditional lectures.

entries.definition: A state of deep engagement in which challenge and skill are well matched and attention is strongly focused on the activity.
entries.why: Designers may seek conditions that support sustained engagement without confusing engagement itself with learning.

entries.definition: Assessment used during learning to generate information that can guide improvement, feedback, instruction, or next steps rather than only certify a final outcome.
entries.why: Continuous formative evidence can help learners and educators make adjustments while learning is still underway.

entries.definition: A vision of learning as a connected, lifelong continuum rather than a series of disconnected episodes, with experiences tailored to individuals across locations, media, organizations, and periods of time.
entries.why: It provides the organizing idea for linking learning science, technology, data, governance, policy, and human infrastructure into one evolving system.

entries.definition: The belief that abilities can develop through effort, effective strategies, feedback, and learning over time.
entries.why: Learner beliefs can affect persistence, response to difficulty, and willingness to engage with feedback.

entries.definition: The principle that people remain responsible for decisions and outcomes in human–AI decision loops and that accountability should not be transferred to an AI system.
entries.why: In education, human accountability preserves teachers’ legitimate responsibility for pedagogical decisions, tool selection, assessment, and student support.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The capacity of people to retain meaningful autonomy, judgement, and control when evaluating and using AI systems rather than allowing AI to displace human decision-making.
entries.why: Protecting human agency is especially important in education because AI can influence teaching, assessment, knowledge construction, and learner autonomy.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The people, roles, practices, and organizational structures that provide guidance, coaching, instruction, facilitation, or other support to learners.
entries.why: Learning performance emerges from social and organizational conditions as well as from software and content.

entries.definition: An approach to design that grounds decisions in an understanding of people, their goals, contexts, constraints, and experiences, using iterative research and testing.
entries.why: Learning systems are more useful when learners and other stakeholders shape the problem definition as well as the solution.

entries.definition: An approach to education that treats learning as a socially intensive human endeavor and uses technology to support relationships among learners, educators, and communities.
entries.why: This framing keeps educational objectives and human relationships ahead of technology selection.

entries.definition: An approach to AI that places human capacities, rights, inclusion, safety, accountability, and sustainable development at the centre of the design, selection, use, and monitoring of AI systems.
entries.why: In education, a human-centred approach keeps AI subordinate to educational and human purposes rather than allowing technical capability alone to determine practice.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: A values- and attitudes-based orientation toward human–AI interaction that keeps human rights, human flourishing, human agency, and human accountability central to the use of AI.
entries.why: A human-centred mindset helps educators evaluate AI in terms of its consequences for people, learning, society, and citizenship rather than only its technical performance.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: The principle that the selection, use, monitoring, and consequential decisions involving AI remain under meaningful human control and human accountability.
entries.why: Human control helps prevent AI systems from displacing legitimate educational judgement or obscuring responsibility for decisions affecting learners.

sources.name: UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers

entries.definition: A philosophy and set of processes for addressing human performance at the system level throughout design, development, operation, and the broader system lifecycle.
entries.why: HSI helps multidisciplinary teams treat people as integral system components and balance human needs with technology, organizational constraints, cost, and lifecycle risk.

entries.definition: An xAPI Group that has its own Inverse Functional Identifier, allowing the Group to be recognized independently of its current member list.
entries.why: An identified Group can remain a stable entity even as membership changes, which matters for team-based learning and organizational records.

entries.term: IEEE 1484.11.1-2022 — Data Model for Content Object Communication
entries.definition: An IEEE standard defining the data model used to exchange learner, interaction, objective, status, timing, preference, and score information between a learning content object and a runtime service, typically within an LMS environment.
entries.why: The standard provides a common runtime data model for LMS-delivered content and forms part of the technical foundation associated with SCORM-style content-to-platform communication.

entries.term: IEEE 1484.11.2-2020 — ECMAScript API for Content-to-Runtime Communication
entries.definition: An IEEE standard defining an ECMAScript application programming interface for communication between learning content and a runtime service, typically supplied by a Learning Management System. It standardizes common API services used to exchange runtime learning data.
entries.why: The API gives browser-based learning content and LMS runtime services a common communication contract and reduces ambiguity in content-to-platform integration.

entries.definition: An IEEE standard defining the conceptual data schema for metadata that describes learning objects, including characteristics such as lifecycle, educational use, technical requirements, rights, relationships, annotations, and classifications.
entries.why: LOM provides a common descriptive model that helps learning technology systems manage, locate, evaluate, exchange, and potentially automate the selection of learning resources.

entries.term: IEEE 1484.12.3-2020 — XML Binding for Learning Object Metadata
entries.definition: An IEEE standard defining a W3C XML Schema binding for the Learning Object Metadata (LOM) data model so LOM metadata instances can be encoded in XML and exchanged consistently between systems.
entries.why: The binding turns the abstract LOM model into an interoperable XML representation that software can validate, exchange, and process consistently.

entries.term: IEEE 1484.13.3-2014 — MPEG-21 Digital Item Declaration Mapping
entries.definition: An IEEE recommended practice mapping elements and attributes from the MPEG-21 Digital Item Declaration model to the IEEE conceptual model for aggregating learning, education, and training resources.
entries.why: Mappings between resource models make it easier for learning systems to interpret and exchange packaged or aggregated digital resources created under different technical specifications.

entries.definition: An IEEE recommended practice mapping the elements and attributes of IMS Content Packaging Information Model Version 1.2 to the IEEE conceptual model for resource aggregation used in learning, education, and training.
entries.why: The mapping helps systems interpret content packages through a shared resource-aggregation model and supports interoperability across packaging approaches.

entries.definition: An IEEE recommended practice mapping the Open Archives Initiative Object Reuse and Exchange (OAI-ORE) Abstract Model and its RDF/XML resource-map representation to the IEEE conceptual model for resource aggregation.
entries.why: It bridges a web-oriented resource aggregation model with the learning-technology resource model, helping preserve meaning when aggregated resources move across technical ecosystems.

entries.term: IEEE 1484.2-2024 — Learning and Employment Record Ecosystems
entries.definition: An IEEE recommended practice for ecosystem-scale systems that issue, hold, present, and exchange Learning and Employment Records (LERs) representing education, skills, employment, and related achievements using interoperable digital credentials and shared services.
entries.why: LER ecosystems connect education and employment data across organizational boundaries, supporting portable records, skills-based hiring, career mobility, and learner-controlled exchange of verified achievements.

entries.definition: An IEEE recommended practice for defining competencies and competency frameworks, including the information needed to describe skills, knowledge, abilities, attitudes, habits of practice, behaviors, and learning outcomes in ways that can support interoperable data.
entries.why: Technical interoperability depends on more than a data format. Organizations also need disciplined, understandable practices for deciding what competencies mean and how they should be defined and reused.

entries.definition: An IEEE standard defining a data model for describing, referencing, and sharing competency definitions, competency frameworks, and rubrics across learning, credentialing, workforce, and employment systems.
entries.why: Common competency identifiers and structures let different systems refer to the same skills, knowledge, abilities, behaviors, and learning outcomes with consistent meaning.

entries.term: IEEE 1589-2020 — Augmented Reality Learning Experience Model
entries.definition: An IEEE standard for interoperable augmented-reality learning systems. It defines a conceptual model for relationships among the physical world, the learner, digital information, learning activities, and the environment, along with data models and XML/JSON bindings for representing activities and context.
entries.why: A common AR learning model supports reusable content, interchangeable components, experience repositories, and learning experiences that can move across otherwise proprietary AR platforms.
entries.aka: IEEE 1589; AR Learning Experience Model; AR-LEM

entries.definition: An IEEE learning technology standard that defines an extensible set of metadata classes and properties for describing learning resources and learning events. Its model is designed to align with Resource Description Framework (RDF) approaches and can be represented in graph-oriented and other formats.
entries.why: Shared metadata terms make learning resources and events easier to describe, discover, exchange, connect, and reuse across systems without forcing every platform to invent its own vocabulary.

entries.term: IEEE 2955-2025 — Self-Learning Tutorials and Side-by-Side Learning
entries.definition: An IEEE recommended practice describing methods for creating self-learning tutorials, including screencast-based and spoken tutorials, with guidance for side-by-side learning techniques.
entries.why: It gives tutorial creators a common, standards-based methodology for designing instructional experiences that learners can follow independently while working alongside the demonstrated task.

entries.definition: An IEEE standard defining a framework for digital intelligence, including digital literacy, skills, and readiness. The framework spans eight areas of digital life — identity, use, safety, security, emotional intelligence, literacy, communication, and rights — across citizenship, creativity, and competitiveness levels.
entries.why: It gives education, government, industry, and other stakeholders a shared vocabulary for describing the competencies people need to participate effectively and responsibly in digital life.

entries.definition: The IEEE standard for the xAPI data model and RESTful web service used to communicate learner and human-performance experience data between activities and a Learning Record Store (LRS). It standardizes the JSON-based model and service behavior derived from xAPI 1.0.3.
entries.why: xAPI provides a common way for heterogeneous learning, performance, simulation, mobile, and other systems to record and exchange experience data outside the boundaries of a single LMS.

entries.definition: An IEEE standards committee that develops and maintains standards for learning technology and related data interoperability.
entries.why: Many specifications used in modern learning data ecosystems are standardized or maintained through LTSC working groups.

entries.definition: The stage in which a learning solution is deployed into its intended environment, monitored, supported, and adjusted based on evidence.
entries.why: Implementation reveals operational constraints and real-world effects that prototypes and laboratory tests may miss.

entries.definition: The use of models to infer latent states, relationships, or explanations from observed data.
entries.why: Learning systems often need to reason about constructs that are not directly observable, such as mastery, engagement, or likely next actions.

entries.definition: A professional who analyzes learning needs and designs, develops, implements, and evaluates instruction, learning experiences, and supporting materials or systems.
entries.why: Instructional designers remain central to modern learning teams, while their role increasingly intersects with technology, data, systems, and multidisciplinary collaboration.

entries.definition: Learning in which an instructor actively guides, structures, supports, or responds to learners as they engage with learning activities.
entries.why: Instructor facilitation can provide timely guidance and social interaction, but instructor time is a limited resource that should be allocated where it most supports learning.

entries.definition: The sensors, software, schemas, event definitions, identifiers, and processes used to observe and record what happens in a system.
entries.why: Instrumentation determines what a learning organization will later be able to measure, analyze, verify, or automate.

entries.definition: A computer-based instructional system that uses automated procedures to guide learners through problems, provide hints, deliver feedback, and adapt support based on learner performance.
entries.why: Intelligent tutors were an important step beyond fixed branching instruction and remain a major foundation for adaptive learning systems.

entries.definition: An xAPI Activity Definition used to describe an interaction such as true-false, choice, fill-in, matching, performance, sequencing, Likert, numeric, or other response formats.
entries.why: Interaction Activities give assessment and practice events a structured representation that can preserve response semantics across systems.

entries.definition: A globally unique identifier format used throughout xAPI to identify things such as Verbs, Activities, Activity types, extensions, and other vocabulary concepts. IRIs can contain international characters and include a scheme.
entries.why: IRIs let independent systems refer to the same concepts without relying on local database identifiers, which is fundamental to semantic interoperability.

entries.definition: In the xAPI standard, an IRL is an IRI that can be translated to a URI that functions as a URL.
entries.why: xAPI distinguishes identifiers from locators because some identifiers merely name concepts while others can also be used to retrieve resources or metadata.

entries.definition: The ability of systems, services, and data to work together through shared interfaces, formats, semantics, and expectations.
entries.why: Interoperability reduces dependence on one platform and allows learning data to retain value across an ecosystem.

entries.definition: An identifier used by xAPI to uniquely identify a particular Agent persona or Group, such as a mailbox, mailbox hash, OpenID, or account.
entries.why: IFIs are the basis for determining when Agent or Group representations refer to the same identity, which affects querying, deduplication, and record continuity.

entries.definition: The part of the learning engineering process in which collected data are analyzed to explore outcomes and determine how well a solution addresses the learning challenge.
entries.why: Investigation turns implementation data into evidence for deciding whether to refine the design, continue implementation, or reframe the problem itself.

entries.definition: A design approach in which solutions are repeatedly created, tested, evaluated, and refined.
entries.why: Iteration makes evidence part of the development process and lowers the cost of discovering that an assumption was wrong.

entries.definition: A lightweight text format for representing structured data using objects, arrays, names, and values.
entries.why: xAPI and many modern learning technology interfaces use JSON to exchange machine-readable data between systems.

entries.definition: A JSON-based linked-data format that maps familiar JSON structures to semantic identifiers and relationships that can be interpreted as RDF.
entries.why: xAPI Profiles use JSON-LD so Profile documents remain approachable as JSON while also participating in linked-data and RDF tooling.
entries.aka: JavaScript Object Notation for Linked Data

entries.definition: A workflow management method that visualizes work, limits work in progress, and supports continuous flow.
entries.why: Learning engineering teams can use Kanban to make bottlenecks visible and coordinate iterative work across disciplines.

entries.definition: The persistence of learned knowledge or skill over time so that it can be retrieved and used later.
entries.why: Durable learning requires more than immediate performance during instruction; design must account for what remains available after time passes.

entries.definition: An xAPI dictionary whose keys are RFC 5646 language tags and whose values are strings in the corresponding languages.
entries.why: Language Maps let the same xAPI concept carry human-readable labels or descriptions in multiple languages while preserving a shared machine-readable identifier.

entries.definition: A UNESCO Institute for Statistics assessment framework for evaluating and strengthening national education data ecosystems across learning assessments, administrative data, survey systems, expenditure data, and review and monitoring.
entries.why: LASER provides a structured approach for identifying gaps in education data quality, coverage, reporting, and alignment with standards and for prioritizing improvements.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: A family of approaches that combine iterative development with attention to flow, waste reduction, rapid feedback, and value delivery.
entries.why: It helps learning engineering teams coordinate complex work while adapting to evidence and changing conditions.

entries.definition: The capacity and opportunity for learners to make choices, exercise control, and take an active role in directing aspects of their own learning.
entries.why: Agency supports active participation and can help learners connect effort, strategy, choice, and responsibility to their progress.

entries.definition: A feedback cycle in which evidence about learner activity or outcomes informs subsequent guidance, practice, support, or system behavior.
entries.why: Fast, relevant feedback can help learners adjust strategies and can help systems personalize future experiences.

entries.definition: A representation of a learner's relevant characteristics, such as knowledge, skills, performance, preferences, goals, context, or other states used to inform instruction or personalization.
entries.why: Learner models provide the information adaptive systems use to decide what support, content, sequence, or intervention may be appropriate next.

entries.definition: The protection and management of privacy interests associated with the collection, modeling, sharing, storage, and use of data about learners and their activities.
entries.why: Digital learning systems can observe detailed behavior across contexts, so privacy affects trust, adoption, personalization, and the legitimacy of data use.

entries.definition: The analysis and use of data from learning environments to understand and improve learning experiences, instructional strategies, and related decisions.
entries.why: Learning analytics converts event data into evidence, but its value depends on instrumentation, measurement validity, interpretation, and responsible use.

entries.definition: A visual interface that presents learning analytics, activity patterns, performance indicators, relationships, or recommended interventions for learners and other stakeholders.
entries.why: Dashboards can turn high-volume learning data into decision support for learners, instructors, administrators, and system teams.

entries.definition: A structured process for measuring learners’ knowledge and skills in specified subject areas at particular ages or grade levels, often to estimate learning outcomes for a wider education system.
entries.why: Learning assessments provide evidence about what students know and can do and can support analysis of learning quality, equity, and system performance.

sources.name: UNESCO UIS National Education Statistical Capacity Assessment

entries.definition: A group of learners who work together on problems or learning goals within physical or virtual spaces supported by shared norms, processes, and scaffolds.
entries.why: Learning communities provide social structures in which learners can discuss, apply, and construct knowledge together.

entries.definition: An umbrella term for practitioners who design learning resources or experiences, including roles such as instructional designer, learning engineer, and learning technologist.
entries.why: The term makes it possible to discuss design practice across job titles while focusing on the shared work of shaping learning experiences.

entries.definition: The structures and processes used to coordinate authorities, policies, resources, standards, support, experimentation, and decision making across a learning ecosystem.
entries.why: Connected ecosystems span many stakeholders and systems, so they need explicit mechanisms for shared decisions, local autonomy, policy enforcement, resourcing, and change.

entries.definition: A professional who applies evidence about human learning and development at scale to create reliable, affordable, data-rich learning environments within real contexts.
entries.why: The role reflects the move from isolated course design toward multidisciplinary, evidence-driven design and operation of complex learning systems.

entries.definition: A process and practice that applies learning sciences, human-centered and engineering design methods, and data-informed decision making to support learners and their development.
entries.why: It provides a multidisciplinary framework for designing, operating, evaluating, and improving learning as a system.

entries.term: Learning Engineering Evidence and Decision (LEED) tracker
entries.definition: A learning-engineering documentation structure for recording design decisions, related justifications, sources of influence, and revisions in connection with the learning engineering process.
entries.why: The tracker externalizes design reasoning so teams can communicate, revisit decisions, support iteration, and study authentic design work without relying only on retrospective recall.

entries.definition: An iterative, concurrent process for addressing learning challenges by framing the context and stakeholders, creating and instrumenting a solution, implementing it in authentic settings, investigating outcomes with data, and refining the work continuously.
entries.why: It organizes learning engineering as an evidence-producing cycle rather than a one-way sequence, so design, implementation, and investigation can inform one another throughout the work.

entries.definition: The person or interdisciplinary group assembled to address a learning challenge, with the mix of skills and knowledge determined by the problem, context, learners, stakeholders, and technical needs.
entries.why: Learning engineering problems often cross disciplinary boundaries, so team composition should follow the challenge rather than a fixed job-title template.

entries.definition: The combined physical, digital, social, organizational, and instructional conditions in which learning occurs.
entries.why: Learning outcomes are influenced by interactions across the environment, not only by the content presented to a learner.

entries.definition: The application of engineering and systems methods to the design, integration, and improvement of learning environments.
entries.why: It brings infrastructure, interfaces, data, and operational conditions into the same frame as instructional design.

entries.definition: A discrete occurrence or interaction that can be observed or recorded as part of a learning or performance experience.
entries.why: Well-defined events make it possible to instrument activity consistently across platforms and analyze what happened over time.

entries.definition: An event associated with learning, broadly interpreted to include formal and informal experiences such as courses, reading, field experiences, self-directed work, or receiving a certificate.
entries.why: xAPI is intentionally designed to track learning beyond a single delivery system or course, so the broad meaning of “learning experience” sets the scope for what can be recorded.

entries.definition: The design of experiences, environments, interactions, and supports intended to help people learn.
entries.why: LXD contributes user-centered and instructional design practices to multidisciplinary learning engineering work.

entries.definition: Structured descriptive information about learning resources, activities, competencies, or related entities.
entries.why: Shared metadata improves discovery, exchange, automation, and the ability to connect resources across systems.

entries.definition: A network of relationships among learners, teachers, parents, and wider communities that supports teaching and learning across institutional boundaries.
entries.why: The source presents EdTech as a means of creating new connections among educational stakeholders rather than merely delivering content.

entries.definition: An organization that develops the capacity to learn from evidence and experimentation, test iterative solutions, and adjust practice based on what is learned.
entries.why: The source applies this idea to ministries of education, emphasizing institutional capacity for experimentation, measurement, and course correction.

entries.definition: A measure of the share of 10-year-old children who cannot read and understand a simple story.
entries.why: The measure provides a system-level indicator of foundational learning challenges and is used in the source to frame the broader learning crisis.

entries.definition: A machine-readable record representing evidence about a learning, training, or performance event, state, milestone, or achievement.
entries.why: Learning records become more portable and useful when they are structured with shared standards and identifiers.

entries.definition: An xAPI Client that retrieves Learning Records from one or more Learning Record Stores for processing such as interpretation, analysis, translation, dissemination, or aggregation.
entries.why: xAPI is not only about sending data into an LRS. LRCs represent the consuming side of the ecosystem, where records are turned into analytics, services, reports, or other downstream uses.

entries.definition: Software or a system component that observes activity and sends standards-based learning event records to a Learning Record Store.
entries.why: Separating event producers from storage helps instrument many systems without requiring all analytics to live inside each source application.

entries.definition: A system that receives, stores, and provides access to xAPI learning records.
entries.why: An LRS is a core component in architectures where learning event data must be collected independently of any single delivery platform.

entries.definition: An interdisciplinary field that studies how people learn and how learning can be supported across cognitive, social, motivational, cultural, and contextual dimensions.
entries.why: Learning engineering uses findings from the learning sciences to inform design hypotheses and evaluation.

entries.definition: A view of learning as continuous across the full lifespan and across formal, nonformal, informal, workplace, community, and lived experiences.
